questions.question:
Rearrange the following parts to complete the sentence that begins: "The museum will remain closed"
A. while the old roof
B. for two months
C. is being repaired
D. from next Monday
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) D, B, A, C
Why: "The museum will remain closed from next Monday (D) for two months (B) while the old roof (A) is being repaired (C)." The "while" clause needs its subject and verb together.
Why not the others: (A) and (B) split "the old roof" from "is being repaired" with "for two months". (C) begins with a verb that has no subject.
Key point: Keep a clause's subject and verb together.

questions.sub_topic: Idioms: bolt from the blue, pull someone's leg, over the moon, sixes and sevens
questions.question:
Match the idioms in List-I with their meanings in List-II:

List-I
(A) A bolt from the blue
(B) To pull someone's leg
(C) Over the moon
(D) At sixes and sevens

List-II
(I) Extremely happy
(II) In confusion and disorder
(III) A complete surprise, usually unwelcome
(IV) To tease someone in a friendly way
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) (A)-(III), (B)-(IV), (C)-(I), (D)-(II)
Why: A bolt from the blue — a sudden surprise (III); pull someone's leg — tease (IV); over the moon — very happy (I); at sixes and sevens — in confusion (II).
Why not the others: (A) swaps the first two; (B) swaps the middle two; (C) swaps the last two.
Key point: Learn idioms as whole units of meaning.

questions.question:
Match the words in List-I with their definitions in List-II:

List-I
(A) Hypocrite
(B) Cosmopolitan
(C) Connoisseur
(D) Fugitive

List-II
(I) A person with expert knowledge and taste in a field such as art or food
(II) A person who runs away, especially from the law
(III) A person who pretends to have virtues he or she does not have
(IV) At home in many countries; including people from many parts of the world
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) (A)-(III), (B)-(IV), (C)-(I), (D)-(II)
Why: Hypocrite — one who pretends to virtue (III); cosmopolitan — of the whole world, as in a cosmopolitan city (IV); connoisseur — an expert judge of taste (I); fugitive — one who flees (II).
Why not the others: (A) swaps hypocrite and cosmopolitan; (B) swaps cosmopolitan and connoisseur; (D) swaps the last two.
Key point: "Cosmo-" means world; "fug-" means flee, as in refuge.

questions.topic: Verbal Ability: Choosing the Correct Word
questions.question:
Choose the correctly spelt word to fill in the blank:
His ________ would not let him keep the wallet he had found.
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) conscience
Why: The correct spelling is c-o-n-s-c-i-e-n-c-e.
Why not the others: (A) misses the "s". (B) misses the "i". (C) misses the second "c".
Key point: Conscience = con + science.

questions.question:
Choose the word most similar in meaning to the word in capitals:
Everyone was ASTONISHED when the youngest player won the tournament.
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) Amazed
Why: Astonished means greatly surprised; amazed means the same.
Why not the others: (A), (B) and (D) describe other feelings.
Key point: An unexpected win causes astonishment.

questions.topic: Verbal Ability: Choosing the Correct Word
questions.question:
Choose the correct preposition to fill in the blank:
Candidates must be proficient ________ at least two Indian languages.
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) in
Why: The standard expression is "proficient in" a skill or language.
Why not the others: (A), (B) and (D) are not standard with "proficient" for languages.
Key point: Proficient in, skilled in, fluent in.

questions.topic: Verbal Ability: Sentence Transformation and Correctness
questions.sub_topic: Correct sentences: prefer to, did come, jury, bread and butter
questions.question:
Which of the following sentences are grammatically correct?
A. I prefer reading to watching television.
B. He did not came to school yesterday.
C. The jury has given its verdict.
D. Bread and butter are my usual breakfast.
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
options: C) A, C and D only
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) A and C only
Why: A uses "prefer ... to" correctly. In C, the jury acts as one body, so "has" and "its" are correct.
Why not the others: B should be "did not come". D should be "is": "bread and butter" is one dish. Options (B), (C) and (D) include B or D.
Key point: Two nouns joined by "and" take a singular verb when they name one thing.

questions.sub_topic: Antonym pairs: accept, ally, rapid, lend
questions.question:
Select the correct pairs of antonyms:
A. accept — reject
B. ally — enemy
C. rapid — swift
D. lend — borrow
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
options: A) A, B, C and D
B) B, C and D only
C) A, B and D only
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) A, B and D only
Why: Accept and reject, ally (friend) and enemy, lend and borrow are opposites.
Why not the others: Pair C is a pair of synonyms — rapid means swift. Options (A), (B) and (D) include pair C.
Key point: Test each pair on its own.

questions.question:
Rearrange the following sentences to form a coherent paragraph:
A. Each colour bends by a slightly different amount.
B. As a result, the white light spreads out into a band of seven colours.
C. When sunlight enters a raindrop, it bends and is reflected inside the drop.
D. This bending separates white light into its different colours.
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) C, D, A, B
Why: C introduces the bending; D says "This bending separates ... colours"; A explains that each colour bends differently; B gives the result.
Why not the others: (A) mentions "each colour" before the colours are introduced. (B) begins with "Each colour". (D) gives the result before the explanation in A.
Key point: "This bending" and "As a result" point back to what came just before.

questions.question:
Rearrange the following parts to form a meaningful sentence:
A. take a holy dip
B. in the river
C. at sunrise
D. On the day of the fair, thousands of pilgrims
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) D, A, B, C
Why: The opener with the subject (D) is followed by the verb (A), where (B) and when (C).
Why not the others: (B), (C) and (D) start with a lower-case part, so the capitalised opener is lost in the middle.
Key point: Subject, verb, place, time.

questions.topic: Verbal Ability: Choosing the Correct Word
questions.question:
Choose the most appropriate word to fill in the blank:
My teacher gave me some useful ________ about choosing a college.
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) advice
Why: After "some useful", a noun is needed; "advice" is the uncountable noun.
Why not the others: (B) "Advise" is the verb. (C) "Advice" has no plural form. (D) is a past form of the verb.
Key point: Advice (noun, with c) and advise (verb, with s).

questions.topic: Verbal Ability: Choosing the Correct Word
questions.question:
Choose the most appropriate word to fill in the blank:
After the famine, thousands of families decided to ________ from Ireland to America.
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) emigrate
Why: "Emigrate" means to leave one's own country to live in another; the sentence speaks of leaving Ireland ("from Ireland").
Why not the others: (A) "Immigrate" means to come into a new country; it is used with "to" or "into". (C) gives "migrate to from Ireland", which is ungrammatical. (D) is a noun.
Key point: Emigrate from; immigrate to.

questions.topic: Verbal Ability: Choosing the Correct Word
questions.question:
Choose the most appropriate word to fill in the blank:
The medicine made him so ________ that he fell asleep in the bus.
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) drowsy
Why: "Drowsy" means sleepy and heavy.
Why not the others: (A), (C) and (D) all suggest being awake or active.
Key point: The result ("fell asleep") decides the word.

questions.question:
Select the words that describe "a person who talks a great deal":
A. loquacious
B. laconic
C. voluble
D. lucid
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
options: B) A, B and C only
D) A, C and D only
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) A and C only
Why: "Loquacious" and "voluble" both describe someone who talks a lot and easily.
Why not the others: B (laconic) means using very few words — the opposite. D (lucid) means clear and describes speech, not quantity. Options (B), (C) and (D) include one of them.
Key point: Laconic and loquacious both begin with "l" but are opposites.

questions.topic: Verbal Ability: Choosing the Correct Word
questions.question:
Choose the most appropriate word to fill in the blank:
Passengers are asked to remain ________ and report any unattended bag to the station staff.
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) vigilant
Why: "Vigilant" means watchful and alert to danger.
Why not the others: (A) means lazy. (B) means too satisfied to notice danger. (D) means unaware.
Key point: Reporting unattended bags requires watchfulness.

questions.question: Choose the one word for: "A place where dead bodies are kept until they are buried or cremated"
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) Mortuary
Why: A mortuary is a room or building where bodies are kept for a short time before burial or cremation.
Why not the others: (A) is a burial ground. (B) is a place for long-term treatment of the sick. (C) is a room where many people sleep.
Key point: "Mort-" means death, as in mortal.

questions.question: Choose the word most similar in meaning to TRIVIAL:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) Unimportant
Why: Trivial means of little value or importance.
Why not the others: (A) only looks similar. (B) and (C) are close to opposites.
Key point: Do not quarrel over trivial matters.

questions.topic: Verbal Ability: Choosing the Correct Word
questions.question:
Choose the most appropriate word to fill in the blank:
Regular exercise helps to ________ the muscles of the back.
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) strengthen
Why: After "to", a verb is needed; "strengthen" means to make strong.
Why not the others: (A) is an adjective. (B) is a noun. (C) is an adverb.
Key point: "-en" turns some nouns and adjectives into verbs: strengthen, widen, deepen.

questions.question: Choose the word most opposite in meaning to DISMAL:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) Cheerful
Why: Dismal means gloomy and depressing; cheerful means bright and happy.
Why not the others: (A) is a synonym. (C) and (D) are unrelated.
Key point: A dismal day is dark and dreary.

questions.question: Choose the word most similar in meaning to INTREPID:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) Fearless
Why: Intrepid means fearless and adventurous.
Why not the others: (B) and (C) only look similar. (D) is the opposite.
Key point: Intrepid explorers go where others fear to go.

questions.topic: Verbal Ability: Sentence Transformation and Correctness
questions.question:
Choose the option that best expresses the sentence in the passive voice:
The children were flying kites on the terrace.
options: A) Kites were flown by the children on the terrace.
B) Kites were being flown by the children on the terrace.
C) Kites are being flown by the children on the terrace.
D) Kites had been flown by the children on the terrace.
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) Kites were being flown by the children on the terrace.
Why: The past continuous "were flying" becomes "were being flown".
Why not the others: (A) is in the simple past. (C) is in the present continuous. (D) is in the past perfect.
Key point: Continuous tenses use "being" in the passive.

questions.sub_topic: Prepositions in sentences: averse, devoid, indulge, consist
questions.question:
Match the sentences in List-I with the prepositions in List-II that fill their blanks:

List-I
(A) He is not averse ____ hard work.
(B) The desert is almost devoid ____ trees.
(C) She rarely indulges ____ sweets.
(D) The team will consist ____ eleven players.

List-II
(I) to
(II) of (meaning "without")
(III) in
(IV) of (meaning "made up of")
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) (A)-(I), (B)-(II), (C)-(III), (D)-(IV)
Why: Averse to (I); devoid of, meaning without (II); indulge in (III); consist of, meaning made up of (IV).
Why not the others: (A) swaps "to" and "in"; (B) swaps the two senses of "of"; (C) gives "indulge of" and "consist in".
Key point: The same preposition can carry different senses; read the meaning given in List-II.

questions.topic: Verbal Ability: Choosing the Correct Word
questions.question:
Choose the most appropriate word to fill in the blank:
Please wait here ________ the doctor calls your name.
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) until
Why: "Until" means "up to the time when".
Why not the others: (B) means "if not". (C) means "from a past time" or "because". (D) shows purpose.
Key point: Wait until something happens.

questions.topic: Verbal Ability: Choosing the Correct Word
questions.question:
Choose the most appropriate word to fill in the blank:
You need the ________ of the principal to leave the school early.
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) permission
Why: "The permission of" needs a noun meaning consent.
Why not the others: (B) as a noun means an official document, which does not fit "of the principal" here. (C) means allowing too much freedom. (D) is an adjective meaning allowed.
Key point: Permission is consent; a permit is a document.

questions.question:
Choose the word most opposite in meaning to the word in capitals:
The FERTILE plains of the Ganga produce a large share of India's wheat.
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) Barren
Why: Fertile land produces good crops; barren land produces little or nothing.
Why not the others: (B) and (D) describe the plains but are not opposites. (C) is close in meaning.
Key point: The opposite of fertile soil is barren soil.

questions.topic: Verbal Ability: Choosing the Correct Word
questions.question:
Choose the most appropriate word to fill in the blank:
________ the shop was closed, we bought the medicine from the hospital pharmacy.
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) Since
Why: "Since" here means "because": the shop being closed is the reason for buying elsewhere.
Why not the others: (A) and (C) show contrast. (B) shows a condition.
Key point: Since can show time or reason; here it shows reason.

questions.question:
Match the phrasal verbs in List-I with their meanings in List-II:

List-I
(A) Break into
(B) Break out
(C) Break off
(D) Break through

List-II
(I) Start suddenly (a fire, war or disease)
(II) Force a way past an obstacle
(III) Enter a building by force
(IV) End a relationship or talks suddenly
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) (A)-(III), (B)-(I), (C)-(IV), (D)-(II)
Why: Thieves break into a house (III); a fire breaks out (I); talks are broken off (IV); the sun breaks through the clouds, or troops break through a line (II).
Why not the others: (A) swaps the first two; (C) swaps break out and break off; (D) swaps the last two.
Key point: One verb, four particles, four meanings.

questions.topic: Verbal Ability: Choosing the Correct Word
questions.question:
Choose the most appropriate word to fill in the blank:
Could you ________ me a favour and post this letter on your way?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) do
Why: The fixed collocation is "do someone a favour".
Why not the others: (A), (C) and (D) do not go with "a favour" in this sense.
Key point: Do a favour, do one's duty, do homework.

questions.question:
Rearrange the following parts to form a meaningful sentence:
A. you will miss
B. Unless you
C. leave the house now,
D. the first bus to the city
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) B, C, A, D
Why: "Unless you (B) leave the house now (C), you will miss (A) the first bus to the city (D)."
Why not the others: (A) gives "Unless you you will miss". (B) starts with a lower-case part. (D) gives "Unless you the first bus".
Key point: Complete the "unless" clause before the main clause.

questions.topic: Verbal Ability: Choosing the Correct Word
questions.question:
Choose the correct preposition to fill in the blank:
Mother was angry ________ me for coming home late.
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) with
Why: One is "angry with" a person and "angry about" or "at" a thing.
Why not the others: (A) and (C) are not standard. (D) repeats "me for", which makes the sentence ungrammatical.
Key point: Angry with a person; angry about a thing.

questions.question:
Match the figures of speech in List-I with the examples in List-II:

List-I
(A) Irony
(B) Litotes
(C) Alliteration
(D) Apostrophe

List-II
(I) She is not a bad singer at all.
(II) O moon, why do you hide behind the clouds?
(III) The swimming coach drowned in the pool.
(IV) The busy bees buzzed by the blue bell.
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) (A)-(III), (B)-(I), (C)-(IV), (D)-(II)
Why: A swimming coach drowning is the opposite of what one expects — irony (III); "not a bad singer" means a good one by denying the opposite — litotes (I); repeated "b" sounds — alliteration (IV); speaking to the moon — apostrophe (II).
Why not the others: (B) swaps irony and litotes; (C) swaps litotes and alliteration; (D) swaps the last two.
Key point: Litotes is understatement by denying the opposite.

questions.topic: Verbal Ability: Sentence Transformation and Correctness
questions.question:
Choose the option that best expresses the sentence in indirect speech:
He said, "Let us go for a walk."
options: A) He said that let us go for a walk.
B) He told that we go for a walk.
C) He suggested that we should go for a walk.
D) He ordered us to go for a walk.
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) He suggested that we should go for a walk.
Why: "Let us" expresses a suggestion; it is reported with "suggested/proposed that we should ...".
Why not the others: (A) keeps the direct form. (B) "told" needs an object and the tense is not shifted. (D) changes a suggestion into an order.
Key point: Let us → suggested that we should.

questions.topic: Verbal Ability: Choosing the Correct Word
questions.question:
Choose the most appropriate phrasal verb to fill in the blank:
The flight was delayed and finally ________ two hours late.
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) took off
Why: An aeroplane "takes off" when it leaves the ground.
Why not the others: (A) means to start a hobby or occupy space. (B) means to take control. (D) means to absorb or deceive.
Key point: Planes take off and land.

questions.topic: Verbal Ability: Choosing the Correct Word
questions.question:
Choose the most appropriate word to fill in the blank:
________ English and Hindi, she can also speak Tamil and Bengali.
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) Besides
Why: "Besides" means "in addition to".
Why not the others: (A) "Beside" means next to. (B) and (D) do not fit the meaning and grammar here.
Key point: Beside = next to; besides = as well as.

questions.question:
Rearrange the following parts to form a meaningful sentence:
A. by the British
B. The bridge, which was built
C. is still used by trains today
D. more than a century ago,
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) B, A, D, C
Why: "The bridge, which was built (B) by the British (A) more than a century ago (D), is still used by trains today (C)." The comma after "ago" closes the "which" clause.
Why not the others: (A) puts the main verb inside the "which" clause and leaves "more than a century ago, by the British" hanging. (C) starts with a lower-case part. (D) puts the main verb inside the "which" clause.
Key point: Punctuation marks where an inserted clause ends.

questions.sub_topic: Where new memories are first held
questions.question:
Read the following passage and answer the question that follows.

Many students believe that the best way to prepare for an examination is to stay up all night with their books. Research on sleep suggests the opposite. Sleep is not simply time when the brain is switched off; it is when the brain does some of its most important work on memory.

During the day, new information is held for a while in a small, curved part of the brain called the hippocampus, which acts rather like a notebook for recent events. At night, especially during deep sleep, the brain appears to replay these memories and move them into the outer layer of the brain, the cortex, where they can be stored for the long term. Scientists call this process consolidation. Later in the night, during the stage known as REM sleep, when most vivid dreams occur, the brain seems to link new memories with old ones, which may help us solve problems and see connections.

A night of sleep passes through several cycles of these stages, each lasting about ninety minutes. Cutting sleep short therefore removes some of the stages in which memories are strengthened. Students who sleep well after learning usually remember more the next day than those who stay awake, and a tired brain also finds it harder to pay attention to new material.

Teenagers generally need eight to ten hours of sleep a night, yet many get far less. Bright screens late at night can delay the body's natural signal for sleep. The advice of sleep researchers is simple: study in the evening, put the phone away well before bedtime, and let the night finish the work.

Question: According to the passage, where in the brain is new information first held for a while?
options: B) In the outer layer of the brain
D) In the stage of REM sleep
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) In the hippocampus
Why: "During the day, new information is held for a while in a small, curved part of the brain called the hippocampus."
Why not the others: (A) and (B) are the same place, where memories are stored for the long term later. (D) is a stage of sleep, not a part of the brain.
Key point: Keep track of which name goes with which role.

questions.question:
Read the following passage and answer the question that follows.

During the day, new information is held for a while in a small, curved part of the brain called the hippocampus, which acts rather like a notebook for recent events. At night, especially during deep sleep, the brain appears to replay these memories and move them into the outer layer of the brain, the cortex, where they can be stored for the long term. Scientists call this process consolidation. Later in the night, during the stage known as REM sleep, when most vivid dreams occur, the brain seems to link new memories with old ones, which may help us solve problems and see connections.

A night of sleep passes through several cycles of these stages, each lasting about ninety minutes. Cutting sleep short therefore removes some of the stages in which memories are strengthened. Students who sleep well after learning usually remember more the next day than those who stay awake, and a tired brain also finds it harder to pay attention to new material.

Teenagers generally need eight to ten hours of sleep a night, yet many get far less. Bright screens late at night can delay the body's natural signal for sleep. The advice of sleep researchers is simple: study in the evening, put the phone away well before bedtime, and let the night finish the work.

Question: Why, according to the passage, does cutting sleep short harm memory?
options: A) It removes some of the stages in which memories are strengthened
B) It makes the hippocampus grow smaller overnight
C) It prevents the brain from dreaming during the day
D) It makes students study for too many hours
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) It removes some of the stages in which memories are strengthened
Why: "Cutting sleep short therefore removes some of the stages in which memories are strengthened."
Why not the others: (B) and (C) are not stated. (D) confuses the cause.
Key point: "Therefore" links a cause to its result.

questions.question:
Read the following passage and answer the question that follows.

Many students believe that the best way to prepare for an examination is to stay up all night with their books. Research on sleep suggests the opposite. Sleep is not simply time when the brain is switched off; it is when the brain does some of its most important work on memory.

During the day, new information is held for a while in a small, curved part of the brain called the hippocampus, which acts rather like a notebook for recent events. Scientists call this process consolidation. Later in the night, during the stage known as REM sleep, when most vivid dreams occur, the brain seems to link new memories with old ones, which may help us solve problems and see connections.

A night of sleep passes through several cycles of these stages, each lasting about ninety minutes. Cutting sleep short therefore removes some of the stages in which memories are strengthened. Students who sleep well after learning usually remember more the next day than those who stay awake, and a tired brain also finds it harder to pay attention to new material.

Teenagers generally need eight to ten hours of sleep a night, yet many get far less. Bright screens late at night can delay the body's natural signal for sleep. The advice of sleep researchers is simple: study in the evening, put the phone away well before bedtime, and let the night finish the work.

Question: As used in the passage, "consolidation" refers to:
options: A) Joining two schools into one
B) Waking up in the middle of a sleep cycle
C) Dreaming about events of the past
D) Moving recent memories into long-term storage
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) Moving recent memories into long-term storage
Why: The passage defines it: the brain replays memories and moves them into the cortex "where they can be stored for the long term. Scientists call this process consolidation."
Why not the others: (A) is another everyday meaning of the word, not the one used here. (B) and (C) are not what the word refers to.
Key point: A technical term is usually explained in the sentence before or after it.

questions.sub_topic: What the writer would advise a student
questions.question:
Read the following passage and answer the question that follows.

Many students believe that the best way to prepare for an examination is to stay up all night with their books. Research on sleep suggests the opposite. Sleep is not simply time when the brain is switched off; it is when the brain does some of its most important work on memory.

During the day, new information is held for a while in a small, curved part of the brain called the hippocampus, which acts rather like a notebook for recent events. At night, especially during deep sleep, the brain appears to replay these memories and move them into the outer layer of the brain, the cortex, where they can be stored for the long term. Scientists call this process consolidation. Later in the night, during the stage known as REM sleep, when most vivid dreams occur, the brain seems to link new memories with old ones, which may help us solve problems and see connections.

A night of sleep passes through several cycles of these stages, each lasting about ninety minutes. Cutting sleep short therefore removes some of the stages in which memories are strengthened. Students who sleep well after learning usually remember more the next day than those who stay awake, and a tired brain also finds it harder to pay attention to new material.

Teenagers generally need eight to ten hours of sleep a night, yet many get far less. Bright screens late at night can delay the body's natural signal for sleep. The advice of sleep researchers is simple: study in the evening, put the phone away well before bedtime, and let the night finish the work.

Question: A student has an examination at nine the next morning. Which plan would the writer most likely approve?
options: A) Study until dawn, then sleep for an hour before the examination
B) Revise in the evening and get a full night's sleep
C) Sleep in the afternoon and study through the night
D) Use a phone app to study in bed until midnight
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) Revise in the evening and get a full night's sleep
Why: The writer advises: "study in the evening, put the phone away well before bedtime, and let the night finish the work."
Why not the others: (A) and (C) cut night sleep. (D) uses a bright screen late at night, which the passage warns against.
Key point: Apply the writer's advice to a new situation.

questions.question:
Read the following passage and answer the question that follows.

Many students believe that the best way to prepare for an examination is to stay up all night with their books. Research on sleep suggests the opposite. Sleep is not simply time when the brain is switched off; it is when the brain does some of its most important work on memory.

During the day, new information is held for a while in a small, curved part of the brain called the hippocampus, which acts rather like a notebook for recent events. At night, especially during deep sleep, the brain appears to replay these memories and move them into the outer layer of the brain, the cortex, where they can be stored for the long term. Scientists call this process consolidation. Later in the night, during the stage known as REM sleep, when most vivid dreams occur, the brain seems to link new memories with old ones, which may help us solve problems and see connections.

A night of sleep passes through several cycles of these stages, each lasting about ninety minutes. Cutting sleep short therefore removes some of the stages in which memories are strengthened. Students who sleep well after learning usually remember more the next day than those who stay awake, and a tired brain also finds it harder to pay attention to new material.

Teenagers generally need eight to ten hours of sleep a night, yet many get far less. Bright screens late at night can delay the body's natural signal for sleep. The advice of sleep researchers is simple: study in the evening, put the phone away well before bedtime, and let the night finish the work.

Question: The tone of the passage is best described as:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) Informative and advisory
Why: The writer explains research on sleep and memory and ends with practical advice.
Why not the others: (A) and (B) The writer does not attack or mock students. (D) There is no sense of regret.
Key point: Factual passages that end with advice are informative and advisory.

questions.question:
Read the following passage and answer the question that follows.

Kalu was a street dog until the winter he followed Neha home from the bus stop and refused to leave. Her father grumbled for a week about the cost of milk, then built him a kennel out of an old cupboard and painted his name on it in red.

On Diwali night, the crackers began at dusk. Kalu, who had never heard such noise, shook under the bed until a rocket burst right outside the window. Then he bolted through the open door and into the dark lanes, and he did not come back.

For nine days the family searched. Neha's brother printed posters with Kalu's photograph and pasted them on every lamp post. Her father, who had once complained about the milk, took his scooter out each evening and rode slowly through the colonies, calling the dog's name. Neha left the gate open at night, against all the rules of the house.

On the tenth morning she found Kalu asleep on the doorstep. He was thinner, his paws were sore and there was a burr caught in his ear, but around his neck was a blue cotton collar that none of them had seen before. Tied to it was a slip of paper. In careful handwriting it said: "He stayed with us at the dairy for a week. He ate well but he would not settle. We think he wanted to go home."

Neha's father read it twice, cleared his throat and went inside. A few minutes later, he came out with a full bowl of milk.

Question: What made Kalu run away from home?
options: A) Neha's father scolded him about the milk
B) The family had gone away for Diwali
C) Another dog chased him into the lanes
D) A rocket burst right outside the window
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) A rocket burst right outside the window
Why: Kalu shook under the bed "until a rocket burst right outside the window. Then he bolted through the open door."
Why not the others: (A) happened much earlier. (B) and (C) are not stated.
Key point: "Then" links the cause to the action.

options: A) He never wanted Kalu and was glad he had gone

Question: The note says, "He ate well but he would not settle." This means that Kalu:
options: A) Refused to eat the food at the dairy
B) Was too ill to walk any further
C) Remained restless and unhappy there
D) Fought with the other animals at the dairy
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) Remained restless and unhappy there
Why: To settle is to become calm and comfortable in a place. Although he ate well, he did not feel at home, so "we think he wanted to go home".
Why not the others: (A) contradicts "ate well". (B) and (D) are not stated.
Key point: "But" signals a contrast with the first half of the sentence.

Question: Neha's father "read it twice, cleared his throat and went inside". This suggests that he:
options: A) Disagreed with what the note said

questions.sub_topic: The market switches on its own small suns
questions.question:
Read the following passage and answer the question that follows.

At dusk the old market changes its face. The office-goers have gone, the shutters of the cloth shops are rattling down, and in their place the evening people arrive: the chaat-sellers with their brass pots, the flower women with heaps of marigold and jasmine, the man who sells balloons shaped like fish.

The light goes first. It slides off the rooftops and lingers for a while on the temple spire, turning it the colour of a ripe apricot, and then it is gone, and the market switches on its own small suns. Bulbs swing on wires above the vegetable carts, kerosene lamps hiss beside the fruit-sellers, and the glass bangles in the bangle shop catch every flame and throw it back, a thousand times brighter.

The noise rises with the dark. Sellers sing out their prices in a tune that has not changed in a hundred years; a bicycle bell argues with a scooter horn; somewhere a radio plays an old film song that nobody is listening to and everybody knows. The air is thick with frying, with coriander, with dust and incense and the sweet, heavy breath of the jasmine.

I have walked through this market a thousand evenings. I know where the pavement is broken and which dog sleeps under which cart. And still, every evening, as the lights come on, I feel I am arriving somewhere for the first time.

Question: "The market switches on its own small suns." What are the "small suns"?
options: A) The marigolds and jasmine of the flower women
B) The bulbs and lamps lit by the sellers
C) The ripe apricots on the fruit carts
D) The reflections on the temple spire
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) The bulbs and lamps lit by the sellers
Why: The next sentence lists them: "Bulbs swing on wires ... kerosene lamps hiss" — the market's own lights after the sun has set.
Why not the others: (A) and (C) are not lights. (D) The light on the spire is the last of the real sun.
Key point: A metaphor is often explained in the very next sentence.

Question: "A bicycle bell argues with a scooter horn." The figure of speech used here is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) Personification
Why: Bells and horns cannot argue; they are given a human action — personification.
Why not the others: (B) There is no "like" or "as". (C) No sound is repeated at the start of words. (D) No contrasting ideas are balanced.
Key point: Human actions given to objects signal personification.

Question: "A radio plays an old film song that nobody is listening to and everybody knows." This suggests that the song:
options: A) Is new and has not yet become popular
B) Is so loud that nobody can bear to hear it
C) Has been banned from the market
D) Is so familiar that people know it without attending
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) Is so familiar that people know it without attending
Why: The song is part of the background; everyone knows it so well that nobody needs to listen.
Why not the others: (A) It is "an old film song". (B) and (C) are not suggested.

Question: What does the writer feel, according to the last paragraph?
options: A) A fresh sense of arrival, though the place is familiar
B) Boredom, because the market never seems to change
C) Fear of the broken pavement and the stray dogs
D) Sadness that the old market will soon be gone
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) A fresh sense of arrival, though the place is familiar
Why: Although the writer knows every broken stone and sleeping dog, "every evening, as the lights come on, I feel I am arriving somewhere for the first time."
Why not the others: (B) is the opposite. (C) and (D) are not stated.
